This notebook tackles multiclass text classification by combining rule-based feature engineering with learned representations from multiple neural and classical models, then ensembling predictions through gradient boosting.

The core strategy is feature stacking: rather than relying on a single text representation, the workflow generates dozens of diverse features—both handcrafted and model-derived—and feeds them to XGBoost as the final learner. This approach is robust because it captures complementary signal from different feature families.

Handcrafted features include author-discriminative vocabulary counts, constructed by computing per-author word frequencies and filtering for words with frequency ratios exceeding a threshold of roughly 2.2 relative to other authors. Additional engineered features capture stylistic patterns: stopword density, word and character counts, mean word length, and per-character punctuation frequencies. Linguistic statistics like duplicate word ratios and author-aligned word counts add fine-grained stylistic markers.

The notebook generates multiple learned representations. It fits a Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier on count vectorized n-grams (1–3 grams) and separately on character-level TF-IDF (1–5 character n-grams), extracting their calibrated probability outputs as three-dimensional features per class. Doc2Vec and spaCy word vectors (300 dimensions each) are appended as dense representations. Character-level TF-IDF is reduced to 20 components via Truncated SVD.

Two neural architectures contribute stacked predictions. A CNN processes 10,000-vocabulary word sequences padded to length 70, using an embedding layer, convolution, pooling, and dense layers. A simplified FastText variant applies global average pooling over embeddings with 2-gram augmentation.

The validation strategy uses stratified K-fold cross-validation (typically 3–5 splits) with log-loss as the metric, applied consistently across all intermediate models. Each fold trains its models independently and averages predictions across folds before feeding to XGBoost, reducing overfitting risk on the held-out validation sets.

The final XGBoost model uses soft probability objective with early stopping (patience 30 rounds), max depth 3, learning rate 0.1, and column subsampling 0.7. These conservative hyperparameters prevent overfitting to sparse feature combinations. The notebook samples 30% of training data early on, suggesting computational constraints drove this choice.

A notable design choice is treating all base learner outputs as tabular features rather than averaging them directly, allowing XGBoost to learn nonlinear interactions and reweight features by importance. This stacking approach generalizes well across text domains where author or category signals may be distributed across stylistic, lexical, and semantic dimensions simultaneously.

Multinomial Naive Bayes is applied separately to count-vectorized word unigrams-to-trigrams and character n-grams (with STOPWORDS excluded), generating six probability columns. This is fed into XGBoost with multi-class softmax loss, max depth 3, column subsampling 0.7, and early stopping over 30 rounds during 4-fold cross-validation. Final test predictions are the average of the four fold predictions, output as a submission CSV with probabilities for each author.

The approach prioritizes diversity: linguistic hand-crafted features, multiple neural architectures with different pooling strategies, and classical statistical models all feed a single gradient-boosted meta-learner, avoiding the risk of any single representation bottlenecking performance.

Both approaches feed MultinomialNB separately, leveraging its suitability for sparse count data and probabilistic outputs suitable for multi-class problems.

Validation uses 10-fold stratified cross-validation with log-loss as the optimization metric for probability calibration. Naive Bayes models are stacked through ensemble averaging across folds, producing probability estimates for each class that are averaged to stabilize predictions.

The final submission averages normalized probabilities from the TF-IDF Naive Bayes model with XGBoost's class probabilities, effectively creating a two-stage ensemble that combines a simple, interpretable baseline with a high-variance non-linear model. This notebook tackles multi-class text classification using a sequence-based deep learning approach. The core strategy combines pre-trained word embeddings with a lightweight LSTM architecture, avoiding the overhead of end-to-end embedding training while capturing sequential dependencies in literary text.

The feature engineering pipeline centers on GloVe 840B 300-dimensional word vectors. Rather than loading all embeddings upfront, the notebook filters the embedding index to only words appearing in the training, validation, and test sets, dramatically reducing memory consumption. Each text sample is converted to a sequence of embedding vectors by tokenizing, lowercasing, removing stopwords and non-alphabetic characters, and looking up word embeddings. Sequences are padded or truncated to a fixed length of 200 tokens; shorter sequences are zero-padded, and longer ones are clipped. This pre-processing ensures uniform tensor dimensions for batch processing.

The model is a single-layer LSTM with 256 hidden units and a 0.1 dropout rate applied after the final hidden state, feeding into a linear layer for three-class output. The design rationale is simplicity: a single LSTM layer with moderate capacity avoids overfitting on what appears to be a moderately-sized dataset, while dropout regularization provides additional insurance. Importantly, the forward pass uses pack_padded_sequence to efficiently handle variable-length inputs by masking padded positions, preventing the LSTM from learning spurious patterns on padding tokens.

Training employs Adam optimization with a learning rate of 0.03 over 2000 epochs with a large batch size of 8000 on GPU. The large batch size is feasible given the filtered embeddings and fixed sequence length. Loss is evaluated via standard cross-entropy with accuracy tracked per epoch on the training split.

The validation and test splits follow the same pre-processing and padding logic, with sequence lengths sorted in descending order before batching—a common technique that improves LSTM efficiency by reducing unnecessary computation within pack_padded_sequence. Final predictions are obtained by passing packed validation and test sequences through the trained model, then applying softmax to generate class probabilities.

A distinctive aspect is the deliberate constraint on sequence length and careful memory management via filtering embeddings to relevant words, making the approach tractable without distributed training or advanced optimization while maintaining the expressiveness of a pre-trained 300-dimensional word space.

A custom tokenizer using TweetTokenizer handles character-level filtering, preserving only alphabetic characters, spaces, and select punctuation, while URL and handle normalization removes noise. The normalized sequences are then tokenized via a pretrained vocabulary and padded to 220 tokens, enabling fixed-size input to the neural network.

Two residual-style dense layers with 512 hidden units (4× LSTM units) further refine features before sigmoid activation across six output classes, enabling independent probability predictions for each toxicity label. The embedding layer uses frozen pretrained weights loaded from disk, anchoring semantic information.

The training strategy employs seed-based ensemble averaging across ten independent model instances. Validation is performed on a 10 percent held-out split, with mean ROC-AUC across all six labels tracked as the primary metric. Final test predictions are the average of predictions from all ten seeds, a simple but effective ensembling approach that typically improves robustness.

Key hyperparameters—batch size of 128, LSTM units of 128, and sequence length of 220—were likely tuned to balance memory constraints with sufficient temporal context. The use of spatial dropout early in the sequence processing and binary crossentropy loss with sigmoid outputs reflects the multi-label rather than multi-class nature of the problem. The solution begins by extracting atomic positions from geometry files, transforming them into fractional coordinates via lattice-vector inversion. A key preprocessing step applies log transformation to atom count (`log(number_of_total_atoms)`) and log1p to both targets, stabilizing the scale of nonlinear relationships. Spacegroup labels are one-hot encoded to capture crystal symmetry information. Derived atomic position features (a0, a1, a2) are extracted from XYZ geometry files and appended to tabular data. ## Modeling Approach

Two independent symbolic regression models are trained for each target (formation energy and bandgap). Each model consists of a single evolved mathematical expression combining trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic operations with learned constant coefficients. The expressions include nested sine, cosine, tanh, and min/max operations applied to feature combinations. Rather than learning unstructured weights, the GP evolves a single closed-form equation for each task—for example, FE1 sums 70 individually weighted sub-expressions, each combining original and derived features through nonlinear transformations. This explicit symbolic structure aids interpretability while maintaining expressiveness through deep operation nesting.

Inverse log1p transformation (`expm1`) recovers predictions in the original scale before submission. This ensemble-and-clip strategy reduces variance and guards against outlier predictions while maintaining interpretability of individual models.

Structural features are normalized implicitly through the learned coefficients and embedded scaling factors within expressions (values like 0.097734, 0.100000). One-hot encoding of spacegroups creates high-dimensional categorical signals that the symbolic expressions then combine via arithmetic operations.
